title: Chemotherapy day unit: weekly symptom reporting, two candidate designs, the investigator withdraws the trial and chooses mixed methods
notes: Ordinary ambiguity: two candidate designs, and the investigator chooses one. A clinical nurse specialist names both a pragmatic trial and interviews, so routing at create is unresolved (family null, basis unresolved; the 875fe59 classifier and the A1-B evidence-mention rule agree). The problem reply omits family (omitKeys) and repeats the constraints word for word, so nothing changes and no issue arises. A fixture search returns seven records (years 2016 to 2024); the appraisal records six source-derived claims whose passages and numbers occur in the cited abstracts, with certainty moderate. The first design reply proposes a pragmatic trial resting on c1 and c5 with two unknown gates; the proposal must not set study.family (S11 with D3), which stays null. The investigator withdraws it (the rollout committee's decision RC-2026-06 removes equipoise) and the revised reply proposes an explanatory sequential mixed methods evaluation resting on c2, c3, c4 and c6 with both gates met on the investigator's approval records; acceptance is a supported positive (selection accepted, action ready) and only then does family become mixed-methods with basis explicit. The withdrawn decision is kept and exported. Record ids were computed by a generator script that loads stableRecordId from src/lib/evidence/records.ts at 875fe59: normalised-DOI hash for records 1, 3, 4, 5, 7 (ev-0e4joc7, ev-1s3ozft, ev-0vq2bzi, ev-0pod5nb, ev-12cag00) and titleYearKey hash for records 2, 6 (ev-0drtzay, ev-16j6bhd). Requires S11 (routing at create, recommendedFamily, selectionStatus, actionStatus, family unchanged by a proposal, basis explicit on acceptance), S13 (appraisal on the production scan path) and D5 (decision status text). Catches: a proposal silently setting the family, a withdrawn decision erased or re-accepted, a default family substituted for an unresolved one, and a choice lost on reload.

inputs.need:
I am a clinical nurse specialist in the chemotherapy day unit of a regional cancer centre. In March 2026 the breast and colorectal clinics started weekly electronic symptom reporting between cycles: patients answer a short set of questions on a tablet or phone, and severe answers (fever, uncontrolled vomiting, diarrhoea more than six times a day, chest pain) send an alert to the triage nurse. The lung and head-and-neck clinics are due to start in January 2027. Eight months in, completion is patchy. In the breast clinic most expected weekly reports come in during the first month and far fewer by the fourth cycle; nurses say some alerts sit unanswered over weekends; and I keep hearing from older patients that they stopped because nobody seemed to read the answers.

I am weighing two designs and would value help choosing between them. We could run a pragmatic trial in the two clinics that have not started yet, giving weekly reporting to half of the new patients and usual telephone triage to the rest, and compare emergency visits and admissions during chemotherapy. Or we could combine the completion and alert data we already hold with interviews with patients who stopped reporting and with the triage nurses, to understand who drops out, why, and what happens to alerts. The centre's rollout committee has already decided that every patient starting chemotherapy will be offered weekly reporting by mid-2027, and I have no research funding beyond one protected day a week.

What I need is a design that tells us whether the programme is working for the people it is meant to help, what to change before the next two clinics start, and how to measure completion and alert response properly.
inputs.constraints: No research funding; the nurse specialist has one protected day a week until December 2027. Interviews must happen during clinic hours or by telephone. The reporting platform cannot be reconfigured before the vendor update in June 2027.

records.title: Weekly web-based symptom reporting during outpatient chemotherapy and emergency department visits: a randomised trial
records.authors: Halvorsen-Mbatha K, Duarte-Whitfield R, Oyelaran-Szabo T
records.abstract: We randomised 612 adults starting outpatient chemotherapy at two centres to weekly web-based symptom reporting with nurse alerts or to usual care, in which patients telephoned the unit when concerned. Over six months, 34 percent of patients in the reporting group and 41 percent in the usual care group had at least one emergency department visit. Health-related quality of life declined less in the reporting group. Completion of expected weekly reports was 83 percent in the first month and 71 percent by month six. Patients over 75 and those without home internet access were underrepresented, and both centres had a dedicated nurse reading alerts.

records.title: Completion of weekly electronic symptom reports after routine rollout in a comprehensive cancer centre
records.abstract: We describe completion of weekly electronic symptom reports in the first year after routine rollout to 1,480 patients receiving chemotherapy. Completion of expected reports was 78 percent in the first month of treatment and 46 percent by month six. Completion was lower in patients aged 75 or over (odds ratio 0.52) and in those living in the most deprived areas (odds ratio 0.61). Patients who received a nurse call after their first severe alert completed more of their later reports. The study could not tell whether falling completion reflected improving symptoms or disengagement from the programme.

records.title: Why patients stop reporting symptoms electronically during chemotherapy: an interview study
records.authors: Nkemelu-Varga A, Pereira-Lindholm C, Watanabe-Osei J
records.abstract: We interviewed 31 adults who had stopped weekly electronic symptom reporting before finishing chemotherapy. Three reasons recurred: feeling that nobody read the answers, questions that did not fit their symptoms, and difficulty with the tablet or phone. Several participants said that they stopped after reporting a severe symptom and receiving no call within the day. Participants valued a named nurse and the option of reporting on paper. Interviews were held at one urban centre, and most participants spoke the majority language, so the views of patients who needed an interpreter are missing.

records.title: Alert burden and response times after introducing electronic symptom monitoring in a chemotherapy day unit
records.abstract: We measured alert volume and nurse response time for 12 months after a chemotherapy day unit introduced weekly electronic symptom reports. The unit received a median of 38 severe-symptom alerts per week. The median time from alert to nurse contact was 3.1 hours on weekdays and 19.5 hours at weekends, when no triage nurse was rostered to read alerts. Nurses reported that 29 percent of alerts concerned symptoms already known to the team. The unit added a weekend review rota in month nine, and the evaluation ended before its effect could be measured.

records.title: Electronic patient-reported outcome monitoring during systemic cancer treatment: a systematic review of randomised trials
records.authors: Achterberg-Kimura E, Fitzgerald-Nwosu P, Lemaire-Castellano D
records.abstract: We searched four databases to 2019 for randomised trials of electronic symptom monitoring during chemotherapy or immunotherapy. In all, 14 trials with 5,210 patients met the inclusion criteria. Emergency department visits were reduced in 6 of the 9 trials that measured them, and quality of life favoured monitoring in 8 of 11. Effects on survival were reported in two trials. Adherence to reporting was described inconsistently, and no trial reported outcomes separately for patients who stopped reporting. Risk of bias was moderate to high because neither patients nor staff could be blinded.

records.title: Tablet versus paper symptom questionnaires among adults aged 75 and over receiving chemotherapy: a cross-sectional comparison
records.abstract: We offered 204 adults aged 75 and over receiving chemotherapy a symptom questionnaire either on paper or on a tablet at the same clinic visit. In all, 57 percent chose paper. Those who chose the tablet completed it in a median of 6 minutes and those who chose paper in 4 minutes. Among tablet users, 18 percent needed help from staff to finish. Choosing paper was associated with living alone and with having no internet access at home. The authors recommend keeping a paper route whenever electronic reporting is introduced for older adults.

records.title: Integrating completion data and patient interviews to evaluate electronic symptom reporting: a mixed methods evaluation in a regional cancer network
records.authors: Okafor-Lindgren B, Castaneda-Hughes M, Yilmaz-Fraser D
records.abstract: We combined 12 months of report completion data from three regional centres with interviews with 24 patients and 11 nurses, and integrated the two strands in a joint display. Completion fell most steeply after the first missed nurse response to a severe alert. Interviews explained the pattern: patients read an unanswered alert as a sign that reporting did not matter. Centres that introduced a same-day response standard recovered completion within three months. The evaluation was not designed to estimate effects on emergency visits, and the centres chose themselves to take part.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Randomised trials and a review of 14 trials show that weekly electronic reporting can reduce emergency visits and protect quality of life under trial conditions with a dedicated alert nurse. In routine care, completion falls steeply by mid-treatment (78 to 46 percent in one centre), more among older and more deprived patients, and qualitative and mixed methods work links stopping to unanswered alerts, with weekend response particularly slow. Older adults often prefer paper. The effectiveness question has randomised answers; the unanswered question is how the programme is delivered and who it loses.
response.gradeRationale: Randomised trials and a review support a benefit on emergency visits (moderate certainty, lowered for lack of blinding and trial staffing); evidence on routine-care completion and its causes is observational and qualitative from single centres (low).
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; six source-derived claims with passages; overall certainty moderate for benefit, low for routine delivery.

steps.note: Appraisal of the seven retrieved records (S13). Certainty moderate is the appraisal's own value over inspected records (G1).

response.reading: The benefit of weekly reporting depends on a loop: a patient reports, a nurse responds, the patient keeps reporting. The retrieved trials show the benefit when the loop is staffed; routine-care evidence shows the loop breaking at the response step, with completion falling after unanswered alerts, especially at weekends and among older and more deprived patients. The local question sits on that loop, not on whether the intervention can work.

store.title: Weekly electronic symptom reporting during chemotherapy: who stops reporting, why, and what happens to alerts

response.overview: Explanatory sequential mixed methods evaluation of weekly electronic symptom reporting in the breast and colorectal clinics: a quantitative strand on completion and alert response for all patients treated from March 2026 to February 2027, followed by a qualitative strand of interviews with patients who stopped reporting and with triage nurses, integrated in a joint display.
response.population: Quantitative: every adult who started chemotherapy in the two clinics between 1 March 2026 and 28 February 2027 and was offered weekly reporting (about 420 patients). Qualitative: 20 to 24 patients who stopped reporting before finishing treatment, sampled by age, deprivation and preferred language, and 10 to 12 triage nurses.
response.exposure: Weekly reporting as delivered; for the mechanism analysis, an unanswered severe alert (no nurse contact recorded within 24 hours) in the previous week.
response.procedures: Monthly platform exports under DA-2026-17 give expected and completed reports and alert timestamps; the triage log gives nurse contact times. Interviews run from March to May 2027 by telephone or in clinic, with interpreters where needed, using a topic guide informed by the quantitative results. Integration uses a joint display that sets each quantitative pattern beside the interview themes that explain or contradict it.

outcomes.measure: Any emergency department visit or unplanned admission during the first 12 weeks, described by completion group
outcomes.why: The outcome patients and the centre care about, described without a causal claim.

response.summary: Sequential mixed methods: completion and alert response for about 420 patients, then 30 to 36 interviews, integrated in a joint display.

response.designSummary: Quantitative strand: descriptive completion estimates and a longitudinal model of weekly completion; qualitative strand: reflexive thematic analysis; integration by joint display.
response.sampleSize: All eligible patients are included, about 420. For an overall completion near 60 percent, 420 patients give a 95 percent confidence interval of about plus or minus 4.7 percentage points (square root of 0.24 over 420, times 1.96). About 420 patients over 12 weeks give about 5,000 patient-weeks, which supports a model of weekly completion with five pre-specified terms. The interview sample of 20 to 24 patients and 10 to 12 nurses is set by information power: a focused aim, purposive sampling across age, deprivation and language, and an analysis of patterns already found in the data.
response.primaryAnalysis: Proportion of expected reports completed over weeks 1 to 12 with 95 percent confidence intervals, by clinic, age group (under 75, 75 or over) and deprivation quintile. Mechanism: mixed-effects logistic regression of weekly completion on an unanswered severe alert in the previous week, adjusted for the severity score of the previous report, age group, deprivation quintile and treatment week, with a random intercept for patient.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Median time to nurse contact after alerts, weekday against weekend; emergency visits and unplanned admissions described by completion tertile without causal inference; interview themes coded with COM-B and set against the quantitative patterns in a joint display.
response.missingData: A missing report is the outcome, not missing data; patients who die or stop chemotherapy leave the denominator at that week; missing alert contact times are reported and treated as unanswered only in a sensitivity analysis.
response.multiplicity: One primary estimate and one pre-specified mechanism model; subgroup estimates are descriptive.
response.software: R (lme4) for the quantitative strand; NVivo for coding; the joint display in a shared spreadsheet.
overfittingGuards: Five model terms fixed before exports are examined
Subgroups limited to age, deprivation and clinic
response.summary: About 420 patients give a completion estimate within about 4.7 points; about 5,000 patient-weeks support the mechanism model; interviews sized by information power.

response.risks: Low. Interviews may touch on distressing symptoms or on feeling ignored; interviewers can pause, and a triage nurse is available if a current symptom is disclosed. Nurses may fear blame for slow responses, so results are reported by shift pattern, never by named nurse.
response.consent: Written or recorded verbal consent for interviews, with information in the patient's preferred language; platform and triage data are used under the approved evaluation, and patients can ask for their data to be excluded.
response.data: Exports are pseudonymised by the informatics lead before analysis; interview recordings are transcribed, de-identified and deleted after checking; data stay on the centre's research drive under REB-ONC-2026-044 and DA-2026-17.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: older patients, people in the most deprived areas, those without home internet and those needing an interpreter are the groups most likely to stop reporting and the least heard in the evidence. The sample deliberately includes them, interviews use professional interpreters, and completion is reported by age, deprivation and preferred language.
response.effectiveness: The evaluation shows where the reporting loop breaks and for whom; it does not re-estimate effectiveness, which trials have addressed.
response.efficiency: Uses existing exports and one protected day a week; interviews by telephone limit travel for patients on treatment.
response.costs: Interpreter fees and transcription, met from the unit's education budget; no other costs.
response.grants: None needed; the joint display could support a later bid to test a response standard across the network.
response.partnerships: Triage nurses, the rollout committee, the platform's informatics lead and two patient partners who stopped reporting during their own treatment.
response.rebPath: Approved by the research ethics board on 2026-09-02 (REB-ONC-2026-044), covering platform data and interviews; any change to the interview guide goes back as an amendment.
response.limitations: Two clinics; confounding by illness severity in the mechanism analysis; interview views may not transfer to the lung and head-and-neck clinics.
response.summary: Approved low-risk evaluation with deliberate inclusion of the patients most likely to stop reporting.

response.partnershipPlan: Two patient partners who stopped reporting during their own treatment co-design the interview guide and review the joint display; triage nurses comment on the alert analysis before it is shared with the rollout committee.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; the centre's patient feedback forms from 2026 are read for comments on the reporting programme.

response.title: Who stops weekly electronic symptom reporting during chemotherapy, and why: an explanatory sequential mixed methods evaluation
response.abstract: Objective: to describe completion of weekly electronic symptom reports and alert response in routine chemotherapy care, and to explain why patients stop reporting. Design: explanatory sequential mixed methods in two clinics of a regional cancer centre, March 2026 to May 2027. Methods: completion and alert timestamps for about 420 patients, a longitudinal model linking unanswered alerts to later completion, and interviews with patients who stopped and with triage nurses, integrated in a joint display. Results and conclusions will follow the analysis.
response.introduction: Randomised trials show that weekly electronic symptom reporting can reduce emergency visits when alerts are answered promptly, but in routine care many patients stop reporting within months. Why they stop, and how alert response contributes, has rarely been studied in the same patients.
response.methods: All patients offered weekly reporting in the breast and colorectal clinics are included. Completion over the first 12 weeks is the primary quantitative outcome; a mixed-effects model links unanswered severe alerts to completion the following week. Interviews with purposively sampled patients and triage nurses explore reasons, and a joint display integrates the strands.
response.results: No data have been analysed yet. The report will present completion by clinic, age, deprivation and language, alert response times by weekday and weekend, the mechanism model, the interview themes, and the joint display.
response.discussion: The discussion will relate the local patterns to the trial evidence, set out the changes to the response standard and the paper route before the remaining clinics start, and state what the evaluation cannot show about effectiveness.
response.limitations: Two clinics; confounding by illness severity; interview findings may not transfer to other tumour groups.
response.conclusion: To be written after integration; it will not claim that weekly reporting reduced emergency visits in this centre.

path.problem.rawNeed:
I am a clinical nurse specialist in the chemotherapy day unit of a regional cancer centre. In March 2026 the breast and colorectal clinics started weekly electronic symptom reporting between cycles: patients answer a short set of questions on a tablet or phone, and severe answers (fever, uncontrolled vomiting, diarrhoea more than six times a day, chest pain) send an alert to the triage nurse. The lung and head-and-neck clinics are due to start in January 2027. Eight months in, completion is patchy. In the breast clinic most expected weekly reports come in during the first month and far fewer by the fourth cycle; nurses say some alerts sit unanswered over weekends; and I keep hearing from older patients that they stopped because nobody seemed to read the answers.

I am weighing two designs and would value help choosing between them. We could run a pragmatic trial in the two clinics that have not started yet, giving weekly reporting to half of the new patients and usual telephone triage to the rest, and compare emergency visits and admissions during chemotherapy. Or we could combine the completion and alert data we already hold with interviews with patients who stopped reporting and with the triage nurses, to understand who drops out, why, and what happens to alerts. The centre's rollout committee has already decided that every patient starting chemotherapy will be offered weekly reporting by mid-2027, and I have no research funding beyond one protected day a week.

What I need is a design that tells us whether the programme is working for the people it is meant to help, what to change before the next two clinics start, and how to measure completion and alert response properly.
